question: Does binarizing embedding vectors (sign-only) while preserving retrieval using Hamming distance improve memory efficiency by ≥50% while maintaining recall@3 ≥58%?
why_matters: Could reduce embedding storage from 600MB to ~75MB (8x compression), freeing RAM for larger context or additional models
Binary embeddings enable faster similarity search using bitwise operations (XOR + popcount) instead of float32 cosine similarity
Maintaining >95% of current recall (58%/61.4%) while achieving 8x compression would dramatically improve mobile RAG feasibility
hypotheses: H1: Binary embeddings achieve recall@3 ≥58.0% (current: 61.4%, allowing 3.4pt drop)
H2: Memory footprint reduces to ≤300MB total for embeddings (current: 600MB)
H3: Retrieval latency improves by ≥30% using Hamming distance vs cosine similarity
setup: Reuse PoC 007 hybrid retrieval harness. Modify embedding pipeline: (1) Generate full EmbeddingGemma embeddings, (2) Binarize by taking sign(embedding_vector), (3) Store as bit-packed arrays, (4) Replace cosine similarity with Hamming distance in retrieval, (5) Keep BM25 component at 0.3 weight, (6) Test on full CUAD dataset (1,325 Q&A pairs). Measure: recall@3, memory (RSS), retrieval latency. Baseline: PoC 007 (61.4% recall, 600MB embeddings).
decision_rule: If H1 (recall ≥58%) AND H2 (memory ≤300MB) both hold: adopt; if H1 fails (recall <55%): reject; otherwise: inconclusive and test with adjusted hybrid weights (increase semantic weight to 0.8-0.9)
source_title: The Sign Code: The Hidden Binary Nature of Deep Networks

question: Does sign-pattern matching between query and context embeddings (binary overlap score) provide a fast pre-filtering mechanism that maintains recall@10 ≥85% while reducing candidate set by ≥60%?
why_matters: Two-stage retrieval (fast binary pre-filter → precise full-embedding rerank) could reduce computational cost on mobile devices
Paper shows sign overlap correlates with generalization; high sign agreement between query-context may predict retrieval relevance
Reducing candidate pool from 1,325 to ~530 items before expensive semantic scoring could improve overall latency by 2-3x
hypotheses: H1: Binary pre-filter achieves recall@10 ≥85% when retrieving top-100 candidates (vs full corpus)
H2: Combined two-stage pipeline (binary filter → semantic rerank) maintains final recall@3 ≥60.0% (current: 61.4%)
H3: End-to-end retrieval latency improves by ≥40% compared to single-stage semantic search
setup: Extend PoC 007 harness with two-stage retrieval: (1) Binarize EmbeddingGemma vectors using sign(), (2) Stage 1: compute Hamming distance between query and all document chunks, select top-K candidates (test K=50,100,200), (3) Stage 2: run full semantic search only on candidates, apply hybrid weighting (0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25), (4) Measure recall@3, recall@10 after stage 1, end-to-end latency. Baseline: PoC 007 single-stage retrieval.
decision_rule: If H1 (recall@10 ≥85%) AND H2 (recall@3 ≥60%) AND H3 (latency improvement ≥40%): adopt; if H2 fails (recall@3 <59%): reject; if only H3 fails: inconclusive (latency not critical for current use case)
source_title: The Sign Code: The Hidden Binary Nature of Deep Networks

question: Does augmenting semantic retrieval with sign-code overlap features (% matching signs between query-chunk embeddings) as a reranking signal improve recall@3 by ≥2 points?
why_matters: Paper demonstrates sign overlap correlates with same-class generalization; analogously, query-chunk sign agreement may predict retrieval relevance better than magnitude-based similarity alone
Lightweight feature (simple XOR count) adds minimal computational overhead while potentially improving ranking quality
Could combine with existing hybrid approach: 0.5 semantic + 0.2 BM25 + 0.3 sign-overlap for improved multi-signal fusion
hypotheses: H1: Hybrid retrieval with sign-overlap feature achieves recall@3 ≥63.4% (current: 61.4%, requiring +2pt gain)
H2: Sign-overlap Pearson correlation with relevance labels is ≥0.25 (indicating predictive signal)
H3: Optimal weight for sign-overlap in [0.2, 0.4] range when combined with semantic (0.4-0.6) and BM25 (0.2-0.3)
setup: Extend PoC 007 harness: (1) Generate binary sign vectors from EmbeddingGemma embeddings, (2) For each query, compute three scores per chunk: cosine similarity (semantic), BM25 score, sign-overlap ratio (# matching signs / embedding dimension), (3) Test weighted combinations via grid search over weights summing to 1.0, (4) Measure recall@3, key-fact accuracy on CUAD dataset. Baseline: PoC 007 (0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25). Also compute correlation between sign-overlap and ground-truth relevance.
decision_rule: If H1 (recall ≥63.4%) holds with statistical significance (p<0.05, paired t-test): adopt; if H1 fails (recall gain <1.0pt): reject; if gain is 1.0-2.0pts: inconclusive, test on broader dataset or with key-fact accuracy tiebreaker (require ≥69% vs current 67.9%)
source_title: The Sign Code: The Hidden Binary Nature of Deep Networks

question: Does deploying an elastic-width Qwen2.5-1.5B (with 50% heads active) improve throughput by ≥40% while maintaining key-fact accuracy ≥65%?
why_matters: 1.75x throughput improvement would enable faster answer generation on mobile, reducing user-perceived latency from ~3-4s to ~2s per query
Reduced active parameters (50% heads) could lower peak memory usage by 15-25%, creating headroom for larger context windows or concurrent queries
Validates whether elastic models can maintain RAG quality on contract QA tasks despite reduced capacity, enabling adaptive performance modes (battery-saver vs high-performance)
hypotheses: H1: Token generation throughput increases by ≥40% (baseline: ~15 tok/s → target: ≥21 tok/s)
H2: Key-fact accuracy remains ≥65.0% (current: 67.9%, acceptable drop: ≤2.9 points)
H3: Peak memory usage decreases by ≥10% (current: ~1.6GB for LLM → target: ≤1.44GB)
setup: Convert Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4 to elastic architecture using HydraLLM pipeline (importance-driven weight reordering + subnetwork training). Test on CUAD dataset with existing PoC 007 retrieval pipeline (hybrid 0.7/0.3). Compare full-width (100% heads) vs 50% heads vs 25% heads. Measure: (1) tokens/second on 50-token generation, (2) key-fact accuracy on 1,325 Q&A items, (3) peak RAM via Xcode Instruments. Baseline: current Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4 at 67.9% accuracy.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt 50%-head configuration as default; if H1 holds but H2 fails (accuracy <65%): test 75% heads configuration; if throughput gain <30%: reject (insufficient benefit for conversion effort); otherwise: inconclusive, requires user studies on acceptable accuracy-speed tradeoffs
source_title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models

question: Does elastic-width EmbeddingGemma (with 75% heads active) reduce embedding latency by ≥30% while maintaining recall@3 ≥59%?
why_matters: Embedding generation is often the bottleneck in retrieval (300M model processes 397 docs), reducing this by 30% could cut total retrieval time from ~800ms to ~600ms
600MB → ~450MB memory footprint creates room for caching more document embeddings in RAM, reducing re-encoding overhead
Establishes whether elastic architectures work for retrieval models, not just generative LLMs, enabling system-wide adaptive optimization
hypotheses: H1: Query embedding latency decreases by ≥30% (baseline: ~40ms/query → target: ≤28ms/query)
H2: Recall@3 remains ≥59.0% (current: 61.4%, acceptable drop: ≤2.4 points)
H3: Document re-encoding time for 397 contracts decreases by ≥25% (baseline: ~12s → target: ≤9s)
setup: Convert EmbeddingGemma 300M to elastic MQA architecture using HydraLLM conversion pipeline. Encode CUAD corpus with 75%, 50%, 25% head configurations. Reuse PoC 007 hybrid retrieval harness (0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25). Test on 1,325 queries. Measure: (1) query embedding time (avg over 100 queries), (2) recall@3, (3) full corpus encoding time. Baseline: current EmbeddingGemma at 61.4% recall. Compare elastic embeddings vs BM25-only fallback.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold at 75% heads: adopt; if H2 fails but 90% heads achieves ≥20% latency reduction with recall ≥60%: adopt 90% configuration; if no configuration meets H2: reject (retrieval quality too sensitive); otherwise: inconclusive, test with larger retrieval depth (k=5)
source_title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models

question: Does dynamic head-width switching (100% heads for complex queries, 50% for simple queries) improve average throughput by ≥25% while maintaining overall accuracy ≥67%?
why_matters: Real-world queries have variable complexity (simple lookups vs multi-hop reasoning), adaptive allocation could optimize the performance-quality tradeoff per query
Enables battery-aware operation: switch to narrow models when battery <20%, preserving user experience while extending device runtime
Tests whether elastic models enable runtime adaptivity beyond static configuration, unlocking a new dimension of mobile optimization
hypotheses: H1: Average end-to-end latency decreases by ≥20% across CUAD query distribution (baseline: ~3.2s → target: ≤2.56s)
H2: Overall key-fact accuracy remains ≥67.0% (current: 67.9%, acceptable drop: ≤0.9 points)
H3: Query classifier achieves ≥80% accuracy in routing complex vs simple queries (measured against manual labels on 200-query sample)
setup: Train lightweight query complexity classifier (LogReg on query length, named entities, question type features) on 200 manually-labeled CUAD queries (complex/simple). Implement routing logic: simple queries → 50% heads, complex → 100% heads. Test on remaining 1,125 queries with elastic Qwen2.5-1.5B from PoC 011. Measure: (1) end-to-end latency (retrieval + generation), (2) key-fact accuracy stratified by query type, (3) classifier accuracy via holdout validation. Baseline: static 100% heads at 67.9% accuracy.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 AND H3 hold: adopt with user-configurable mode (auto/performance/efficiency); if H3 fails (<75% routing accuracy): reject dynamic switching, adopt static 75% heads instead; if H2 fails: reject (accuracy loss unacceptable); otherwise: inconclusive, requires A/B testing with real users
source_title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models

question: Does LLM-as-a-judge reranking of top-K retrieved chunks improve key-fact accuracy by ≥5 points while maintaining <4s latency?
why_matters: Paper shows +90% nDCG@10 improvement with reranking, suggesting substantial gains possible even with smaller models
Current system may retrieve relevant chunks but present them in suboptimal order, degrading LLM answer quality
On-device LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B) already loaded, so reranking adds minimal memory overhead
hypotheses: H1: Key-fact accuracy improves by ≥5 points (current: 67.9%)
H2: Recall@3 remains ≥60% (current: 61.4%, ensuring retrieval quality maintained)
H3: End-to-end latency increases by ≤2s (baseline ~2s, target <4s total)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness. After hybrid retrieval returns top-10 chunks, use Qwen2.5-1.5B to score relevance of each chunk (0-2 scale) with prompt: 'Rate relevance of this passage to question [Q]: [chunk]. Score 0=irrelevant, 1=somewhat relevant, 2=highly relevant.' Rerank top-10 by scores, select top-3 for final RAG. Compare key-fact accuracy and recall@3 against baseline (no reranking). Measure latency overhead for 100 queries.
decision_rule: If H1 and H3 hold: adopt; if H1 fails (gain <3 points) or H3 fails (latency >5s): reject; otherwise: inconclusive and test smaller rerank window (top-5 instead of top-10)
source_title: Jev-as-a-Judge for Brazilian Portuguese Information Retrieval: Relevance Assessment and Reranking

question: Does two-stage retrieval (BM25 recall → semantic rerank) improve recall@3 by ≥3 points compared to hybrid fusion?
why_matters: Paper demonstrates effectiveness of reranking BM25 candidates rather than direct fusion
Two-stage approach may better leverage strengths: BM25 for broad recall, embeddings for precision
Could reduce embedding computation by only scoring BM25 top-K instead of full corpus
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 improves to ≥64.4% (current: 61.4%, +3 point threshold)
H2: Key-fact accuracy improves to ≥70% (current: 67.9%)
H3: Retrieval latency remains ≤1.5s (ensuring no performance regression)
setup: Modify PoC 007 harness. Stage 1: BM25 retrieves top-20 chunks. Stage 2: Compute embeddings only for these 20 chunks and rerank by semantic similarity to query. Select top-3. Compare recall@3, key-fact accuracy, and latency against current hybrid (0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25) baseline across full CUAD test set (1,325 Q&A items).
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt; if H1 fails (recall <62%): reject; if H2 fails but H1 holds: inconclusive, test with top-30 BM25 candidates
source_title: Jev-as-a-Judge for Brazilian Portuguese Information Retrieval: Relevance Assessment and Reranking

question: Does relevance-score filtering (LLM judges each chunk before RAG) improve precision without degrading recall@3 below 58%?
why_matters: Paper shows LLM can effectively judge relevance at individual document level (52-65% exact agreement with humans)
Filtering low-relevance chunks before RAG may reduce noise and improve answer quality
Could enable dynamic K selection (use 1-3 chunks based on relevance scores rather than fixed top-3)
hypotheses: H1: Key-fact accuracy improves to ≥70% (current: 67.9%, +2.1 point threshold)
H2: Recall@3 remains ≥58% (allowing 3.4 point degradation as precision trade-off)
H3: Average chunks used per query ≤2.5 (demonstrating noise reduction)
setup: Extend PoC 007 harness. After hybrid retrieval returns top-5 chunks, use Qwen2.5-1.5B to score each (0-2 scale). Include only chunks scoring ≥1 in RAG context, up to 3 chunks maximum. If no chunks score ≥1, use top-1 by retrieval score. Measure key-fact accuracy, recall@3 (whether answer exists in filtered chunks), average chunks used, and latency across CUAD dataset.
decision_rule: If H1 holds and H2 holds: adopt; if H1 fails (<69% accuracy) or H2 fails (<56% recall): reject; if H1 holds but H2 borderline (56-58%): inconclusive, test with threshold ≥0.5 instead of ≥1
source_title: Jev-as-a-Judge for Brazilian Portuguese Information Retrieval: Relevance Assessment and Reranking

question: Does SETAREH-based embedding compression reduce memory footprint by ≥30% while maintaining recall@3 ≥59% (−2.4 points acceptable)?
why_matters: EmbeddingGemma embeddings (768-dim) are computed/cached for 397 documents with ~2000+ chunks; reducing dimension by 30-50% could save 180-300MB of RAM for embedding cache
Enables caching more chunks in memory or running larger models by freeing up embedding storage budget
If successful, could batch-compress all document embeddings offline once, then compress query embeddings on-device with minimal latency overhead
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 with SETAREH-compressed embeddings (50% sparsity) is ≥59.0% (current baseline: 61.4%)
H2: Memory footprint for embedding storage decreases by ≥30% (from ~600MB to ≤420MB for cached embeddings)
H3: Query-time embedding compression adds ≤50ms latency per query (acceptable for mobile UX)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 hybrid retrieval harness. Implement SETAREH transform: (1) Apply Haar wavelet + sorting to all 768-dim EmbeddingGemma embeddings, (2) Retain top-k coefficients (test k=384, 256, 192 for 50%, 66%, 75% sparsity), (3) Compute approximate cosine similarity for semantic retrieval, (4) Combine with BM25 at 0.7/0.3 ratio. Measure recall@3, key-fact accuracy, memory usage (embedding cache size), and per-query latency on CUAD 1,325 Q&A items. Baseline: current 61.4% recall@3 with full 768-dim embeddings.
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt (memory savings justify small accuracy loss); if recall@3 <57% (>4 point drop): reject (accuracy degradation too severe); if H2 fails (memory reduction <30%): reject (insufficient benefit); otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: SETAREH Transform: A Sorting-Assisted Haar-Wavelet Sparsification Method for Approximate Inner-Product Computation

question: Does SETAREH-accelerated batch reranking of top-10 candidates improve recall@3 by ≥3 points while fitting in RAM budget?
why_matters: Current system retrieves top-3 directly; reranking top-10→3 with more precise scoring could improve recall, but computing 10 full LLM embeddings/scores is expensive
SETAREH could enable approximate scoring of 10 candidates cheaply, then full scoring of top-3, combining retrieval quality with efficiency
Demonstrates SETAREH's utility for multi-stage retrieval pipelines common in production RAG systems
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 with SETAREH-based reranking improves to ≥64.4% (+3 points from 61.4% baseline)
H2: Peak memory usage stays ≤5.5GB (within 6GB iPhone 15 Pro budget with 500MB safety margin)
H3: Per-query latency increases by ≤200ms compared to direct top-3 retrieval
setup: Extend PoC 007 harness with two-stage retrieval: (1) Stage 1: Retrieve top-10 candidates using current 0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25 hybrid method, (2) Stage 2: Apply SETAREH transform to cross-encoder or embedding-based reranking scores (compress reranking model's final layer weights), compute approximate scores for all 10 candidates, select top-3. Compare against baseline (direct top-3) and oracle (full reranking with no compression). Measure recall@3, key-fact accuracy, memory peak, and latency on CUAD dataset.
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt (reranking improves quality within constraints); if H1 fails (<63% recall): reject (insufficient improvement for added complexity); if H2 fails (OOM): reject (not feasible); otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: SETAREH Transform: A Sorting-Assisted Haar-Wavelet Sparsification Method for Approximate Inner-Product Computation

question: Does SETAREH-compressed BM25 term-vector representation enable higher weight for BM25 (0.5 vs 0.3) while reducing memory by ≥25%, improving recall@3 by ≥2 points?
why_matters: PoC 010 showed BM25-only achieves 46% recall; hybrid 0.7/0.3 gets 61.4%. Increasing BM25 weight could help, but BM25 inverted indices consume significant memory for large vocabularies
SETAREH could compress BM25 term vectors (sparse high-dimensional representations) for each document, enabling more aggressive BM25 weighting without memory explosion
Addresses the semantic/lexical balance problem: current system may under-utilize lexical matching due to memory constraints on BM25 indices
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 with SETAREH-compressed BM25 (0.5 weight) is ≥63.4% (+2 points from 61.4% baseline)
H2: BM25 index memory footprint reduces by ≥25% (from current size to ≤75% of baseline)
H3: Hybrid retrieval with 0.5 BM25 weight outperforms 0.3 weight by ≥1.5 points in recall@3
setup: Modify PoC 007 BM25 implementation: (1) For each document, represent BM25 term weights as high-dimensional sparse vector (vocabulary size ~10k-50k), (2) Apply SETAREH transform to compress term vectors by retaining top-k Haar coefficients (test 25%, 40%, 50% retention), (3) Compute approximate BM25 scores using compressed vectors, (4) Test hybrid weights: 0.5 semantic + 0.5 BM25, 0.6/0.4, 0.4/0.6. Measure recall@3, key-fact accuracy, BM25 index size, and query latency on CUAD dataset. Baseline: 0.7/0.3 with full BM25 achieving 61.4% recall@3.
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt (better lexical matching with memory savings); if H1 fails (<62% recall): reject (accuracy doesn't justify complexity); if H2 fails (<20% memory reduction): reject (insufficient memory benefit); otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: SETAREH Transform: A Sorting-Assisted Haar-Wavelet Sparsification Method for Approximate Inner-Product Computation

question: Does a two-pass retrieve-then-refine approach (retrieve → generate draft → identify gaps → retrieve again → final answer) improve key-fact accuracy by ≥3 points over single-pass retrieval?
why_matters: SRCoT's core insight is that exposing intermediate drafts and missing-information markers enables better retrieval targeting
Mobile RAG systems often retrieve irrelevant chunks on first pass; a second targeted retrieval could fix this without model changes
Minimal memory overhead (reuses same 3 chunks, just changes which ones) fits within 6GB constraint
hypotheses: H1: Key-fact accuracy reaches ≥70.9% (current: 67.9%, +3 point threshold)
H2: Recall@3 maintains ≥60.0% (current: 61.4%, allowing 1.4 point drop for quality gains)
H3: Total inference time remains ≤3.0x single-pass baseline (acceptable for 2 retrieval + 2 generation passes)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness. Pass 1: retrieve 3 chunks with hybrid search, generate draft answer with Qwen2.5-1.5B prompted to mark [MISSING: topic] gaps. Pass 2: extract missing topics, retrieve 3 new chunks targeted to gaps using BM25 on gap terms + 0.5 weight on original query, generate final answer. Measure key-fact accuracy, recall@3 (whether any pass retrieved correct chunks), and end-to-end latency. Baseline: current single-pass system (67.9% accuracy).
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt; if H1 fails (accuracy <69.0%) or H3 fails (time >3.0x): reject; if H1 marginal (69.0-70.9%) and H3 passes: inconclusive, run extended eval
source_title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs

question: Does adding explicit claim-evidence verification (LLM checks if retrieved chunks support each answer sentence) reduce hallucination rate by ≥25% relative to baseline false-fact rate?
why_matters: SRCoT's claim-evidence mapping provides inspectability and could catch unsupported statements before user sees them
Current 67.9% key-fact accuracy implies ~32% error rate; reducing this directly improves trust
Verification pass reuses already-loaded model and chunks, minimal memory impact
hypotheses: H1: False-fact rate (100% - key-fact accuracy) decreases by ≥25% (from 32.1% to ≤24.1%)
H2: Key-fact accuracy increases by ≥8 points (67.9% → ≥75.9%)
H3: Inference time increases by ≤1.5x baseline (one additional verification pass acceptable)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness. After generating answer, add verification pass: split answer into claims (sentences), prompt Qwen2.5-1.5B to rate each claim as 'supported', 'unsupported', or 'uncertain' given retrieved chunks. Remove or mark uncertain/unsupported claims. Measure key-fact accuracy on final output, compute false-fact reduction, measure latency overhead. Baseline: 67.9% accuracy, no verification.
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt; if H2 fails (<72.0% accuracy, <4 point gain): reject; if H2 marginal (72.0-75.9%) and H3 passes: inconclusive, test on extended dataset
source_title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs

question: Does separating retrieval into 'context' (BM25 on full query) vs 'evidence' (semantic search on extracted answer-relevant terms) stores improve recall@3 by ≥3 points?
why_matters: SRCoT separates provenance-labeled stores (persistent knowledge, experience, short-term memory); adapting this to hybrid retrieval could better match chunk types to query needs
Current hybrid 0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25 is fixed; adaptive weighting based on query characteristics could outperform
No model changes, only retrieval logic modification within existing memory budget
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 reaches ≥64.4% (current: 61.4%, +3 point threshold)
H2: Key-fact accuracy maintains ≥66.9% (current: 67.9%, allowing 1 point drop)
H3: Retrieval time remains ≤1.2x baseline (acceptable for two parallel retrievals merged)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness with modified retrieval: (1) 'Context store': BM25 retrieval on full query → 2 chunks; (2) 'Evidence store': extract key entities/terms from query using simple heuristics (nouns, legal terms), semantic search on these → 1 chunk. Merge to 3 total chunks with deduplication. Measure recall@3, key-fact accuracy, retrieval latency. Baseline: single hybrid retrieval (61.4% recall).
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt; if H1 fails (<63.4% recall): reject; if H1 marginal (63.4-64.4%) and H3 passes: inconclusive, test alternative entity extraction methods
source_title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs

question: Does a prelude-recurrent-coda sandwich architecture for the LLM improve key-fact accuracy by ≥3 points while staying within 6GB RAM?
why_matters: Looped models can achieve better performance with fewer resident parameters (75% reduction shown in paper), critical for mobile deployment
Improved reasoning on context-extraction tasks directly maps to RAG answer quality from retrieved chunks
If successful, could enable larger effective model depth without increasing memory footprint
hypotheses: H1: Key-fact accuracy is ≥70.9% (current: 67.9%, target: +3 points)
H2: Peak memory usage remains ≤6.0GB during inference (current: ~2.6GB for LLM + embeddings)
H3: Latency per query increases by ≤30% (acceptable trade-off for accuracy gain)
setup: Convert Qwen2.5-1.5B to Huginn-style looped architecture: train/find a 1.5B looped model with prelude-recurrent-coda structure, or test existing looped models (e.g., smaller Huginn variants). Use PoC 007 harness with same hybrid retrieval (0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25), measure key-fact accuracy on CUAD dataset, profile memory and latency on iPhone 15 Pro. Baseline: current Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4 (67.9% accuracy).
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 hold: adopt; if H1 fails (accuracy <69.9%) or H2 fails (OOM): reject; if H1 holds but latency >50% increase: inconclusive
source_title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design

question: Does adding input injection at intermediate layers of Qwen2.5-1.5B improve context utilization and boost recall@3 by ≥2 points?
why_matters: Paper shows input injection primarily enhances knowledge retrieval and context utilization - directly relevant to RAG
Can be implemented via prompt engineering or model modification without full retraining
May help LLM better leverage all 3 retrieved chunks rather than focusing on first chunk
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 improves to ≥63.4% (current: 61.4%, target: +2 points)
H2: Key-fact accuracy improves to ≥69.9% (current: 67.9%, target: +2 points)
H3: Implementation adds ≤200ms latency per query
setup: Test modified inference where retrieved chunks are injected at both initial prompt and mid-layer (if model architecture allows), or simulate via multi-stage prompting (first pass with chunk 1, second pass with chunks 2-3 + previous output). Use PoC 007/009 harness, measure recall@3 and key-fact accuracy on CUAD. Baseline: current single-stage retrieval (61.4% recall, 67.9% accuracy).
decision_rule: If H1 or H2 holds and H3 holds: adopt; if both H1 and H2 fail: reject; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design

question: Does implementing a lightweight MoE-style retrieval strategy (routing queries to specialized vs general retrievers) improve recall@3 by ≥3 points?
why_matters: Paper demonstrates MoE models show more balanced expert routing and improved performance on knowledge tasks
CUAD contains diverse contract types - specialized retrievers per contract category could improve precision
Enables parameter-efficient scaling: multiple small specialized embedders vs one large general one
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 improves to ≥64.4% (current: 61.4%, target: +3 points)
H2: Total memory for multiple specialized embedders stays ≤800MB (current: 600MB for EmbeddingGemma)
H3: Routing overhead adds ≤100ms per query
setup: Cluster CUAD documents by contract type (e.g., NDA, service agreement, license). Train/fine-tune 3-4 smaller embedding models (e.g., 100-150MB each) specialized per cluster, plus a lightweight router (classify query → select embedder). Use PoC 007 harness, compare MoE retrieval vs baseline EmbeddingGemma on recall@3. Baseline: 61.4% recall with single 600MB embedder.
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 and H3 all hold: adopt; if H1 fails (recall <63.0%): reject; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design

question: Does multi-granularity retrieval (chunk + document-level summaries) improve recall@3 by ≥4 points over chunk-only retrieval?
why_matters: Addresses the paper's core insight that essential information may be fragmented across different abstraction levels
Document summaries could provide context that connects fragmented chunk-level evidence
Minimal memory overhead: summaries are generated once and stored, likely <100MB for 397 documents
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 with hybrid granularity retrieval ≥65.4% (current: 61.4%)
H2: Key-fact accuracy ≥71.0% (current: 67.9%)
H3: Total memory usage ≤2.2GB including summaries (current: 1.6GB)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness. Generate document-level summaries using Qwen2.5-1.5B (1 paragraph per document). Store summaries as separate embeddings. At retrieval: (a) retrieve top-3 chunks using current hybrid method, (b) retrieve top-1 document summary, (c) combine both for context. Measure recall@3 and key-fact accuracy on CUAD Q&A items. Baseline: current chunk-only retrieval (61.4%).
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 both hold: adopt; if H1 fails by >2 points OR H3 fails: reject; otherwise: inconclusive and test retrieval ratio variations
source_title: From Relevant Memories to Sufficient Evidence: Rethinking Memory Utilization in LLM Agents

question: Does explicit source-grounded answer formatting (citing chunk IDs) improve key-fact accuracy by ≥3 points without reducing recall?
why_matters: Implements paper's 'source-grounded reification' concept to force LLM to ground answers in retrieved evidence
May reduce hallucination by requiring explicit citation of sources
Zero memory overhead: only changes prompt structure
hypotheses: H1: Key-fact accuracy with citation prompting ≥70.9% (current: 67.9%)
H2: Recall@3 ≥60.4% (allowing 1-point degradation, current: 61.4%)
H3: Answer generation latency increases by ≤20% (maintaining usability)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness. Modify prompt to require format: 'Answer: [text] | Sources: [chunk_1, chunk_2]'. Instruct LLM to only use information from cited chunks. Compare against current free-form answer generation. Measure key-fact accuracy (primary) and recall@3 (secondary) on CUAD dataset. Baseline: current prompting (67.9% accuracy).
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 both hold: adopt; if H1 fails by >1 point: reject; if H2 fails by >2 points: reject; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: From Relevant Memories to Sufficient Evidence: Rethinking Memory Utilization in LLM Agents

question: Does query-guided re-ranking of retrieved chunks based on evidential role classification improve key-fact accuracy by ≥5 points?
why_matters: Adapts paper's 'evidential role' concept to prioritize chunks that directly answer vs provide context
Could surface better evidence within the same recall@3 budget
Testable with lightweight classification: use Qwen2.5 to score each chunk's relevance to query before passing to final answer generation
hypotheses: H1: Key-fact accuracy with re-ranking ≥72.9% (current: 67.9%)
H2: Recall@3 remains ≥61.0% (allowing 0.4-point degradation, current: 61.4%)
H3: End-to-end query latency increases by ≤30% (current baseline + re-ranking step)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness. After initial hybrid retrieval of top-5 chunks, use Qwen2.5 with lightweight prompt to score each chunk 0-10 for 'directly answers query'. Re-rank and select top-3. Compare final key-fact accuracy against baseline top-3 selection. Measure on CUAD dataset. Baseline: current hybrid retrieval without re-ranking (67.9% accuracy).
decision_rule: If H1 and H2 both hold: adopt; if H1 fails by >2 points OR H3 fails: reject; otherwise: test with different scoring prompts
source_title: From Relevant Memories to Sufficient Evidence: Rethinking Memory Utilization in LLM Agents

question: Does replacing Q4 Qwen2.5-1.5B with a ternary-quantized version reduce memory footprint by ≥40% while maintaining key-fact accuracy within 3 points of baseline?
why_matters: 50%+ memory reduction could free 500+ MB for larger embedding models or context windows
4 orders of magnitude lower weight-update traffic enables practical on-device fine-tuning for domain-specific contracts
Ternary weights ({-1, 0, +1}) enable 2-bit storage vs current 4-bit, potentially doubling model capacity under same RAM budget
hypotheses: H1: Ternary Qwen2.5-1.5B memory footprint is ≤600 MB (current Q4: 1.0 GB)
H2: Key-fact accuracy is ≥64.9% (current: 67.9%, tolerance: -3 points)
H3: Recall@3 is ≥59.4% (current: 61.4%, tolerance: -2 points)
setup: Convert Qwen2.5-1.5B to ternary weights using quantization-aware training or post-training quantization. Reuse PoC 007 evaluation harness on CUAD dataset (1,325 Q&A items). Measure: (1) actual RAM usage via Xcode Instruments, (2) key-fact accuracy, (3) recall@3. Baseline: current Q4 model (1.0 GB, 67.9%, 61.4%). Test with same hybrid retrieval (0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25, 3 chunks).
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 AND H3 all hold: adopt; if H2 fails by >5 points (accuracy <62.9%): reject; if H1 fails (memory >700 MB): reject; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models

question: Does applying ΣΔ-Sampler for on-device fine-tuning of EmbeddingGemma on CUAD contracts improve recall@3 by ≥3 points while fitting in 6GB RAM budget?
why_matters: Domain-specific fine-tuning could adapt generic embeddings to contract terminology without cloud dependency
50%+ training memory reduction (per paper) makes fine-tuning feasible on-device with only 6GB RAM
Establishes path to continuous learning as new contract types are encountered in production
hypotheses: H1: Fine-tuned EmbeddingGemma recall@3 is ≥64.4% (current: 61.4%, target: +3 points)
H2: Peak training memory usage is ≤5.5 GB (leaving 500 MB system overhead)
H3: Fine-tuning completes in ≤24 hours on-device or convergence is reached within 10 epochs
setup: Implement ΣΔ-Sampler optimizer for EmbeddingGemma 300M fine-tuning on CUAD document corpus (397 documents). Use 80/20 train/validation split of 1,325 Q&A items. Measure: (1) recall@3 on validation set, (2) peak memory via Xcode Instruments during training, (3) training time. Baseline: current frozen EmbeddingGemma (61.4% recall@3). Retain hybrid retrieval and Q4 Qwen2.5-1.5B LLM unchanged.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt; if H1 fails (recall <63.0%): reject; if H2 fails (memory >5.8 GB causing crashes): reject; if H3 fails but H1/H2 hold: inconclusive (impractical training time)
source_title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models

question: Does binary quantization (1-bit) of EmbeddingGemma reduce memory by ≥60% while maintaining recall@3 within 5 points of baseline?
why_matters: Reducing embedding model from 600 MB to <250 MB frees budget for 7B-class LLM or 4x larger context window
Binary embeddings enable 8x faster dot-product similarity via XNOR+popcount operations on ARM NEON
Validates extreme quantization feasibility for retrieval models where ranking matters more than absolute similarity values
hypotheses: H1: Binary EmbeddingGemma memory footprint is ≤240 MB (current: 600 MB, target: 60% reduction)
H2: Recall@3 is ≥56.4% (current: 61.4%, tolerance: -5 points)
H3: Embedding computation time is ≤50% of baseline (enabling faster indexing or real-time retrieval)
setup: Quantize EmbeddingGemma to 1-bit weights using post-training quantization or train binary version using paper's ΣΔ-Sampler if time permits. Reuse PoC 007-009 evaluation harness on CUAD (1,325 Q&A items, 3 chunks). Measure: (1) model size on disk and RAM usage, (2) recall@3 with hybrid retrieval (0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25), (3) average embedding latency. Baseline: current EmbeddingGemma 300M (600 MB, 61.4% recall@3).
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 AND H3 all hold: adopt; if H2 fails (recall <58.0%): reject; if H1 fails (memory >300 MB): reject; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models

question: Does adding perplexity-based answer uncertainty scoring improve hallucination detection (AUROC ≥0.70) without degrading key-fact accuracy by >2 points?
why_matters: Paper shows perplexity achieves 0.81-0.91 AUROC for detecting unsupported claims, allowing runtime flagging of uncertain answers
Mobile users need confidence indicators to know when RAG answers are reliable vs. when they should verify independently
Detection enables fallback strategies (e.g., retrieve more chunks, warn user) for high-uncertainty responses
hypotheses: H1: Perplexity computed on Qwen2.5-1.5B answers achieves ≥0.70 AUROC distinguishing correct from incorrect answers (baseline: random=0.50)
H2: Key-fact accuracy remains ≥65.9% when using perplexity-filtered answers (current: 67.9%, -2pt threshold)
H3: Perplexity computation adds ≤150ms latency per answer on iPhone 15 Pro
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness with hybrid retrieval. For each CUAD Q&A: (1) Generate answer with Qwen2.5-1.5B, (2) Compute token-level perplexity during generation, (3) Label answers as correct/incorrect using key-fact accuracy metric, (4) Calculate AUROC for perplexity as hallucination classifier, (5) Test threshold-based filtering (reject high-perplexity answers) impact on accuracy. Baseline: no filtering (67.9% accuracy).
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt perplexity scoring; if H1 fails (AUROC <0.65): reject; if H2 fails (accuracy drops >2pts): mark inconclusive and test calibration adjustments; if H3 fails: reject for mobile
source_title: When Does Uncertainty Measure RAG Hallucination Risk?

question: Does varying retrieval depth from 1→2→3 chunks improve uncertainty calibration (measured by ECE) by ≥0.05 while maintaining recall@3 ≥60%?
why_matters: Paper shows detection quality can weaken with only top-1 passage, then recover with top-2, revealing when uncertainty scores are meaningful
Understanding optimal retrieval depth for uncertainty calibration could guide dynamic chunk selection strategies
Better calibration means more reliable confidence scores for mobile users deciding whether to trust answers
hypotheses: H1: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) improves by ≥0.05 when moving from top-1 to top-2 chunks (requires establishing ECE baseline)
H2: Recall@3 remains ≥60.0% across all retrieval depths tested (current: 61.4%)
H3: Perplexity-based AUROC increases by ≥0.08 from depth-1 to depth-2, indicating improved uncertainty signal
setup: Extend PoC 009 (retrieval depth testing). For retrieval depths {1, 2, 3}: (1) Retrieve k chunks using hybrid retrieval, (2) Generate answers with Qwen2.5-1.5B, (3) Compute perplexity-based confidence scores, (4) Measure ECE by binning confidence scores and comparing predicted vs actual accuracy, (5) Measure recall@k and AUROC for hallucination detection. Baseline: depth-3 with 61.4% recall, ECE and AUROC to be established.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt depth-2 as optimal for calibrated uncertainty; if H3 holds but H1 fails: inconclusive (uncertainty improves but calibration unclear); if H2 fails: reject (accuracy loss too high)
source_title: When Does Uncertainty Measure RAG Hallucination Risk?

question: Does combining perplexity with semantic-drift (cosine distance between answer embedding and retrieved chunk embeddings) improve hallucination AUROC by ≥0.05 over perplexity-only?
why_matters: Paper demonstrates combined uncertainty + semantic-drift improves calibration over uncertainty alone
Semantic drift detects when generated answer diverges from retrieved evidence, catching a complementary hallucination pattern
EmbeddingGemma already loaded (600MB), so drift computation reuses existing infrastructure with minimal overhead
hypotheses: H1: Combined score (0.6×perplexity + 0.4×semantic_drift) achieves ≥0.75 AUROC for hallucination detection vs. perplexity-only baseline
H2: AUROC improvement is ≥0.05 over perplexity-only approach (requires PoC 011 baseline)
H3: Semantic drift computation adds ≤200ms latency per answer on iPhone 15 Pro
setup: Build on PoC 011 (perplexity scoring). For each CUAD answer: (1) Compute perplexity as before, (2) Embed generated answer using EmbeddingGemma, (3) Calculate cosine distance to embeddings of each retrieved chunk (already computed during retrieval), (4) Aggregate semantic drift (mean or max distance), (5) Test weighted combinations of perplexity + drift, (6) Measure AUROC vs perplexity-only and accuracy impact. Baseline: perplexity-only AUROC from PoC 011.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt combined scoring; if H2 fails (improvement <0.03): reject as not worth complexity; if H3 fails: reject for mobile; if H1 holds but H2 inconclusive (0.03-0.05 gain): test on broader dataset
source_title: When Does Uncertainty Measure RAG Hallucination Risk?

question: Does iterative BM25-only retrieval with term expansion from top-1 chunk improve recall@3 by ≥3 points vs current hybrid retrieval?
why_matters: Eliminates 600MB embedding model, freeing RAM for larger LLM or more context
Reduces cold-start latency by ~200-500ms (no embedding computation)
Paper shows BM25-only SAG2 achieves 86-99% recall@10 on multi-hop tasks, suggesting lexical methods can compete when done iteratively
hypotheses: H1: Two-hop BM25 (initial query → extract terms from top-1 → re-retrieve) achieves ≥58% recall@3 (current hybrid: 61.4%, previous BM25-only: 46%)
H2: Peak RAM usage decreases by ≥500MB (current: ~1.6GB with embeddings)
H3: Mean retrieval latency increases by ≤150ms vs current hybrid (acceptable for RAM savings)
setup: Reuse PoC 007/010 harness with CUAD dataset. Implement 2-stage retrieval: (1) BM25 on original query, take top-1 chunk; (2) extract noun phrases + key terms (regex/spaCy-lite), expand query; (3) BM25 re-retrieve, take top-3. Compare recall@3, RAM (profiler), and latency vs PoC 007 baseline. Test term extraction strategies: all nouns, TF-IDF top-5 terms, named entities.
decision_rule: If H1 holds (≥58% recall@3) AND H2 holds (≥500MB savings): adopt for memory-constrained config. If H1 fails (<55% recall@3): reject. If 55-58% recall@3: inconclusive, test on larger chunk retrieval (recall@5)
source_title: SAG2: Embedding-Free Multi-Hop Retrieval with BM25 and JEV

question: Does a lightweight hybrid approach (BM25 + on-device query embedding only, no corpus embeddings) improve recall@3 by ≥2 points vs pure BM25 while reducing RAM by ≥400MB vs current hybrid?
why_matters: SAG2 eliminates corpus embeddings but the paper doesn't test query-time semantic signals; this explores middle ground
Reduces storage/RAM for corpus embeddings (600MB → 0MB) while keeping semantic query understanding
Query embedding (1 vector) is 100-1000x cheaper than corpus re-embedding, enabling dynamic re-ranking
hypotheses: H1: BM25 retrieval (top-10) + re-rank by cosine similarity to query embedding (select top-3) achieves ≥60% recall@3 (current: 61.4%, pure BM25: 46%)
H2: Peak RAM usage decreases by ≥400MB (no corpus embeddings loaded, only model for single query encoding)
H3: Mean retrieval latency is ≤100ms vs current hybrid (simpler: no weighted combination, just re-rank)
setup: Reuse PoC 007/008 harness. Load EmbeddingGemma only for query encoding (not corpus). At query time: (1) BM25 retrieve top-10 chunks; (2) encode query with EmbeddingGemma; (3) compute cosine similarity against the 10 chunks (encode on-the-fly); (4) return top-3. Measure recall@3, RAM, latency. Compare to PoC 007 baseline and PoC 010 BM25-only.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt (best of both worlds). If H1 fails (<59% recall@3): reject. If H2 fails (<300MB savings): inconclusive, test lazy loading strategies
source_title: SAG2: Embedding-Free Multi-Hop Retrieval with BM25 and JEV

question: Does SQLite FTS5 with BM25 scoring replace the current BM25 implementation with ≥1% recall@3 improvement and ≥30% latency reduction?
why_matters: SAG2 uses SQLite as sole infrastructure; FTS5 provides optimized BM25 with auxiliary indexes
Consolidates storage (no separate BM25 index), potentially reducing memory fragmentation
FTS5 ranking functions and prefix queries might improve contract-specific term matching (legal language has many compound terms)
hypotheses: H1: SQLite FTS5 BM25 achieves ≥46.5% recall@3 when used alone (current BM25-only: 46%, validates parity)
H2: Hybrid retrieval with FTS5 BM25 (0.7 semantic + 0.3 FTS5) achieves ≥62% recall@3 (current: 61.4%)
H3: Mean retrieval latency for BM25 component decreases by ≥30% (FTS5 is C-optimized with better indexing)
setup: Reuse PoC 007 harness and CUAD dataset. Implement FTS5 table with content + metadata columns, enable BM25 ranking. Test: (1) FTS5-only baseline (compare to PoC 010); (2) 0.7 semantic + 0.3 FTS5 (compare to PoC 007). Measure recall@3, component latency (profile BM25 execution time separately), and database file size. Consider FTS5 tokenizers (unicode61 vs porter).
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt (strictly better). If H2 holds but H3 fails: adopt if recall gain ≥1 point (quality over speed). If H1 fails (<45.5%): reject (implementation regression). Otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: SAG2: Embedding-Free Multi-Hop Retrieval with BM25 and JEV

question: Does disagreement-based routing between Qwen2.5-0.5B (weak) and Qwen2.5-1.5B (strong) improve key-fact accuracy by ≥3 points while keeping strong-model usage ≤40%?
why_matters: Enables dynamic quality-cost tradeoff: use 0.5B model (faster, less power) for easy queries, 1.5B only when needed
Requires no ground-truth supervision during inference—routing decisions based purely on model disagreement signals
Could reduce average inference time by 40-60% while maintaining or improving accuracy on difficult queries
hypotheses: H1: Key-fact accuracy with disagreement routing is ≥70.9% (baseline: 67.9%, target: +3 points)
H2: Strong model (1.5B) usage rate is ≤40% of queries at disagreement threshold calibrated for target accuracy
H3: On queries where models agree, weak model accuracy is ≥75% (validating that agreement signals correctness)
setup: Reuse PoC 007-009 harness with CUAD dataset. Deploy Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4 (~650MB, fits with embeddings in 6GB). For each query: (1) generate 2-3 responses from weak model with temperature=0.8, (2) measure self-disagreement (pairwise token-level or semantic similarity), (3) if disagreement exceeds threshold τ, route to strong model, (4) measure final key-fact accuracy and routing rate. Baseline: always use strong model (67.9%). Sweep τ ∈ [0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9] to find optimal tradeoff.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold at any threshold τ: adopt with that threshold; if H1 fails by >2 points at all thresholds: reject; if H2 fails (routing >40%) but H1 holds: inconclusive (consider cost-accuracy tradeoff); otherwise: reject
source_title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing

question: Does weak-model multi-sampling (3 responses) with majority voting improve key-fact accuracy by ≥2 points compared to single-response baseline without routing?
why_matters: Tests the paper's foundation: multiple weak-model responses can improve reliability through local inference
Cheaper than routing to strong model—3x inference on 0.5B model (~150ms) still faster than 1x on 1.5B (~200ms)
Establishes whether disagreement among weak responses is a useful signal for answer quality
hypotheses: H1: Majority-vote accuracy using Qwen2.5-0.5B (3 samples, temp=0.8) is ≥69.9% (baseline 0.5B single: ~65%, target: +2)
H2: When all 3 samples agree, accuracy is ≥78% (validating agreement as correctness signal)
H3: Total inference time for 3x 0.5B samples is ≤250ms per query (vs ~200ms for 1x 1.5B)
setup: Reuse PoC 007-009 harness. Deploy Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4. For each query: generate 3 responses with temperature=0.8, extract key facts from each, use majority voting (≥2/3 agreement) for final answer. Measure key-fact accuracy against single-sample baselines (0.5B and 1.5B). Measure per-query latency. Baseline: Qwen2.5-0.5B single-shot (~65% estimated), Qwen2.5-1.5B single-shot (67.9%).
decision_rule: If H1 AND H3 hold: adopt as foundation for disagreement routing; if H1 fails: reject multi-sampling approach; if H3 fails (latency >250ms): inconclusive, investigate optimization; otherwise: reject
source_title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing

question: Does disagreement-based selective retrieval (route to deeper retrieval when weak model shows high self-disagreement) improve recall@3 by ≥2 points while keeping avg retrieval depth ≤4 chunks?
why_matters: Applies weak-to-strong routing concept to retrieval stage: use shallow retrieval (3 chunks) normally, deeper retrieval (5-7 chunks) only when needed
Reduces LLM context size and inference time for easy queries while improving difficult query performance
Addresses retrieval bottleneck: PoC 009 found deeper retrieval helps some queries but hurts average performance
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 with adaptive retrieval (3 chunks default, 5-7 when disagreement detected) is ≥63.4% (baseline: 61.4%, target: +2)
H2: Average retrieval depth across all queries is ≤4.0 chunks (baseline: 3.0, allowing 25% queries to use 7 chunks)
H3: On queries triggering deep retrieval (high disagreement), recall improvement is ≥5 points vs shallow retrieval
setup: Reuse PoC 007-009 harness. First pass: retrieve 3 chunks, generate 2 preliminary answers with Qwen2.5-1.5B (temp=0.8), measure disagreement. If disagreement > threshold τ: retrieve 4 additional chunks (total 7), regenerate answer with full context. Else: use 3-chunk answer. Measure recall@3, average chunk count, and conditional recall improvement. Baseline: fixed 3-chunk retrieval (61.4% recall). Sweep τ ∈ [0.4, 0.6, 0.8].
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold at any threshold: adopt; if H1 fails by >1 point: reject; if H2 fails (avg depth >4.5): reject due to cost; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing

question: Does replacing EmbeddingGemma 300M with a frozen 16MB vocabulary table maintain recall@3 ≥58% while reducing embedding memory by ≥500MB?
why_matters: Could free 500+ MB RAM (83% reduction from 600MB to ~100MB), enabling larger LLM or deeper retrieval on device
Frozen embeddings eliminate fine-tuning overhead and enable instant vocabulary extension for domain-specific contracts
16MB frozen table could be cached in faster memory tiers, potentially improving retrieval latency by 2-3x
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 is at least 58% (current: 61.4%, accept 3-point drop)
H2: Key-fact accuracy is at least 64% (current: 67.9%, accept 4-point drop)
H3: Embedding memory footprint is at most 120MB (current: 600MB, target 80% reduction)
setup: Generate frozen vocabulary table from EmbeddingGemma using PCA projection and sign binarization per paper method. Reuse PoC 007 hybrid retrieval harness with 0.7 semantic + 0.3 BM25 on CUAD dataset. Compare frozen table vs current EmbeddingGemma on 1,325 Q&A items. Measure recall@3, key-fact accuracy, memory usage (XCTest memory profiler), and embedding computation time.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 AND H3 all hold: adopt; if H1 fails (recall <58%): reject; if H3 fails (memory >120MB): reject; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models

question: Does a frozen embedding vocabulary table improve rare contract term handling by ≥10% on out-of-vocabulary legal terms compared to EmbeddingGemma?
why_matters: Paper shows frozen tables win by 1.7-2.3 nats on rare words, critical for specialized contract terminology
Legal contracts contain domain-specific terms (indemnification clauses, force majeure) that may be poorly represented in general embeddings
Frozen table accepts 10k new words with 3% cost vs 43% collapse for learned tables, enabling post-deployment vocabulary extension
hypotheses: H1: Recall@3 on questions containing rare legal terms (frequency <100 in CUAD) improves by at least 5 points
H2: Overall recall@3 remains at least 58% (current: 61.4%)
H3: Adding 500 contract-specific terms maintains <5% performance degradation
setup: Generate frozen vocabulary from EmbeddingGemma embeddings. Identify rare legal terms in CUAD (frequency <100 occurrences). Create test subset of Q&A pairs containing these terms (~200 items). Test frozen table vs EmbeddingGemma on rare-term subset and full dataset. Simulate vocabulary extension by adding 500 domain terms and re-measuring recall. Use PoC 007 harness with hybrid retrieval.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 hold: adopt; if H1 fails (rare term improvement <2 points): reject; if H2 fails: reject; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models

question: Does combining frozen 16MB embeddings with Qwen2.5-1.5B reduce total model footprint to ≤1.1GB while maintaining key-fact accuracy ≥65%?
why_matters: Total system reduction from 1.6GB to 1.1GB (31% savings) opens headroom for larger context windows or multiple model variants
Simplified deployment: frozen embeddings require no fine-tuning infrastructure, only one-time PCA projection
Paper's BitNet results suggest frozen embeddings work well with quantized models, validating compatibility with Q4 LLM
hypotheses: H1: Total on-device memory (embedding + LLM) is at most 1.1GB (current: 1.6GB, target 500MB reduction)
H2: Key-fact accuracy is at least 65% (current: 67.9%, accept 3-point drop)
H3: End-to-end query latency increases by at most 15% (frozen table may have different compute characteristics)
setup: Implement frozen embedding table generation from EmbeddingGemma. Integrate with existing Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4 LLM. Reuse PoC 007-009 infrastructure for full pipeline test on CUAD dataset. Measure total memory footprint using Xcode Instruments, key-fact accuracy on 1,325 Q&A items, and end-to-end latency (embedding + retrieval + generation) for 100 sample queries.
decision_rule: If H1 AND H2 AND H3 all hold: adopt; if H2 fails (accuracy <63%): reject; if H1 fails (memory >1.2GB): inconclusive; otherwise: inconclusive
source_title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
